newsitem.title: UK: Direct Line motor insurance growth slows.
newsitem.headline: Direct Line motor insurance growth slows.

text.p: Royal Bank of Scotland's Direct Line, the low cost British motor insurer, has this year responded to the highly competitive state of the British motor market by consolidating after ten years of rapid expansion.

While the insurer has issued 528,000 new motor policies over the year to end September, the total number of policies in force has remained at about 2.2 million after ten years of sharp gains, chief executive Ian Chippendale told Reuters.
Total household insurance policies, meanwhile, have risen to around 800,000 -- a gain of ten percent, said Chippendale.
This slowdown in net motor policy growth marks a significant change for the company, which based its strategy on selling as many policies as possible by undercutting competitors on price.

Direct Line pioneered the sale of motor insurance over the telephone. By cutting out brokers from the insurance selling chain and using advertising to raise awareness among consumers, it has profited hugely from its aggressively priced operation.
Founder Peter Wood started out with just 20 million pounds in capital from the Royal Bank of Scotland eleven years ago and now the insurer sells a motor policy every six seconds of the working day.
In the last financial year profits topped 110 million pounds and premium income exceeded 660 million.

But its own success may have contributed in part to the pressure it now faces from other insurers, some of whom have copied its approach and established direct selling operations, while abandoning practices which made them less competitive.

Profits at the interim stage this year fell to five million pounds from 45 million -- most insurers have suffered from the current downturn in the underwriting cycle during which rates have fallen by some 20 percent over three years -- and the stock market is waiting for full year figures due on November 28.
"The market is going through a difficult period, probably the most difficult period in its history," said Chippendale.
"But if we're feeling the pinch, how are these guys doing?" he asked, stabbing a finger at a bar chart illustrating Direct Line's number one position in the market at the end of 1995.

Chippendale said there was no reason why Direct Line's position relative to its competitors should have altered this year. He noted that the company's motor expense ratio far outstripped that of all other insurers at the end of last year and cost per policy has improved to 45 stg from 48 stg.
He added Direct Line has applied selective rate increases of a few percentage points since mid-1996 and argued there were "signs that rates are firming up in the motor sector".

One leading insurance analyst, however, has warned in a report published this week that there is unlikely to be a significant upswing in private motor insurance rates for at least two years and underwriting results will deteriorate in 1997, with losses representing over 11 percent of premiums. "Rates may edge ahead over the next twelve months but there are too many players looking to grow and too few who are content to consolidate," said Merrill Lynch analyst Steven Bird.
"UK general insurance remains in the midst of a cyclical downturn and on balance the news flow should be negative."
Bird said that while Direct Line has been consolidating its position this year, a couple of the composite insurers have been bolstered by development of their own direct writing operations.

"Direct Line has had to face a difficult choice. To continue to grow but see negative impact on current profitability or to enjoy the relatively high returns on renewal business. With so many players looking to grow it appears to have chosen the latter course," he said.
